theBigPicture: The biggest story today is a fragile calm in the Middle East: oil shipments through the Persian Gulf have returned to normal levels, but Iran is threatening to choke them off again unless the US meets its demands. Meanwhile, Brazil is voting in a razor-thin presidential race, and thousands of protesters in Pakistan are marching on the capital demanding the release of jailed opposition leader Imran Khan. For your wallet, the key takeaway is that gas prices remain inflated by war worries even though financial markets themselves are calm.

householdImpact.energyAndFuel: Oil still carries a 'war premium' — Brent crude sits near $114 a barrel even after a $6 drop today — so expect pump prices to stay elevated for now. Home energy bills should hold steady since natural gas remains in its normal price range.
householdImpact.borrowingAndMortgages: Financial markets are calm and lending conditions are easy, which should keep mortgage rates from jumping in the short term. But if high oil prices push up the cost of everyday goods, expect credit card, auto loan, and mortgage rates to stay higher for longer.
householdImpact.groceriesAndSupplyChain: Expensive oil makes it costlier to ship and truck food, and continued attacks on vessels near the Red Sea force cargo onto longer, pricier routes. That cost slowly trickles into your grocery bill, especially for imported items.
householdImpact.jobsAndSavings: Stock markets are steady and financial stress gauges are low, so 401(k)s and retirement accounts should be holding up well. The main risk to your savings and job security is a renewed oil spike that reignites inflation and forces companies to tighten spending.

globalFlashpoints.summary: No major new developments in the past 24 hours, as global attention has shifted to the Middle East and other flashpoints.

Oil flows through the Persian Gulf are back to prewar levels, but Iran threatens to keep the world's most important oil shipping lane shut, Yemen's government launched a major offensive against Iran-backed fighters who claim a strike on Saudi oil facilities, and Israeli strikes continue in southern Lebanon and the West Bank.
No significant new military activity reported in the region over the past day.

Thousands of supporters of jailed Pakistani leader Imran Khan are marching on Islamabad past government roadblocks, France is closing up to 500 schools ahead of renewed student protests, and Brazil's knife-edge election is keeping political tensions high.

topStories.headline: Oil Shipments Back to Normal — But Iran Threatens to Slam the Door Again
topStories.whyItMatters: Persian Gulf oil flows have recovered, yet Iran says it will keep the world's most important oil shipping lane closed until the US meets its conditions. Every day that threat lingers keeps a war premium baked into the price you pay at the pump.

topStories.headline: Brazil Votes in a Photo-Finish Presidential Race
topStories.whyItMatters: Left-wing incumbent Lula faces Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president, in a contest so close a runoff looks likely. The outcome will steer policy in one of the world's biggest food and commodity suppliers, which touches prices far beyond Brazil's borders.

topStories.headline: Yemen Government Launches Major Offensive Against Iran-Backed Fighters
topStories.whyItMatters: The Yemeni government is trying to retake all territory held by the Iran-backed Houthi group, which claims it struck Saudi oil giant Aramco. More fighting near critical shipping lanes means higher risk for global trade and fuel costs.

topStories.headline: Pakistan on Edge as Thousands March to Free Jailed Ex-PM Imran Khan
topStories.whyItMatters: After government talks collapsed, supporters are trekking toward the capital while authorities set up roadblocks to stop them. A deepening political crisis in a nation of 240 million people adds uncertainty to an already tense world.

topStories.headline: France Shuts Up to 500 Schools as Student Protests Resume
topStories.whyItMatters: The education minister cites safety concerns as organizers call for renewed demonstrations. It is a visible sign of growing domestic unrest inside a major Western economy.

topStories.headline: Major Oil Producers Hold Output Steady Despite Middle East Tensions
topStories.whyItMatters: The group of big oil-producing nations chose not to pump extra supply to offset the war-driven price spike. That means supply stays tight and prices at the pump are likely to remain elevated.

whatWeAreWatching: Whether Iran follows through on its threat to keep the Strait of Hormuz shut — the single biggest factor for your gas price right now.
Brazil's first-round election results and the likelihood of a runoff between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro.
How far the Imran Khan protest march gets before it reaches Islamabad, and whether authorities crack down or negotiate.
Progress of Yemen's offensive against the Houthis and any new attacks on ships or oil facilities in the Red Sea.
Iran's internal economic strain after its oil minister resigned and a top security official warned of a dire crisis — economic pressure could change Tehran's willingness to cut a deal.
